Abstract Background  Maternal immunization against respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) offers a promising strategy to reduce severe respiratory infections and hospitalizations among infants, particularly in low- and middle-income countries such as Viet Nam. Administered during antenatal care (ANC), success of maternal RSV immunization programs depends on alignment of ANC visits with vaccine timing recommendations. Methods  We conducted a retrospective cross-sectional study at 15 health facilities across levels of care in Viet Nam. Records from ANC registers for women attending at least one visit in 2023 were included. We analyzed gestational age at ANC visits, visit frequency, and attendance within two vaccine eligibility windows: the window used in Viet Nam (24–36 weeks’ gestation) and the World Health Organization (WHO)-recommended window (≥ 28 weeks' gestation). Results  Among 7,349 women, ANC attendance and visit frequency varied by level of care. Women attending primary facilities had recorded ANC visits earlier (13 weeks’ gestation) and attended more frequently (median four visits) than those at secondary (38 weeks’, median one visit) and tertiary facilities (32 weeks’, median one visit). Attendance within RSV vaccine eligibility windows also differed by level of care. At primary facilities, 47% of women had at least one recorded visit during Viet Nam’s eligibility window, increasing to 88% under the WHO-recommended window. At secondary facilities, 26% had a recorded visit during Viet Nam’s window compared to 85% under the WHO window, while at tertiary facilities, corresponding proportions were 36% and 69%, respectively. Daily vaccine-eligible ANC attendance varied by level of care, with higher-level facilities receiving more eligible women. Conclusions  This study demonstrates the importance of aligning maternal RSV immunization strategies with ANC attendance patterns across levels of care in Viet Nam. Primary facilities, characterized by earlier and more frequent ANC engagement, are critical platforms for maternal vaccination. Adopting the wider WHO-recommended eligibility window, strengthening early ANC counseling, expanding public-sector access, and improving digital continuity of care are essential to achieving equitable national rollout.

Timing is everything: optimizing maternal RSV immunization through ANC attendance patterns and timing in Viet Nam

Background Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is the leading cause of severe respiratory infections and hospitalizations in infants and young children worldwide, responsible for 33 million severe infections and 101,000 deaths annually among children under five years of age [1]. The great­ est risk of severe RSV disease is in the first six months after birth. A disproportionate burden occurs in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). In southern Viet Nam, RSV prevalence in 2019–2021 was 19.6% among children under two years old who sought care at a major pediatric referral hospital for respiratory tract infections [2]. Another study in northern Viet Nam reported RSV prevalence from 2017 to 2020 at 28% for children under five who were hospitalized with severe acute respiratory infection, with the highest burden among infants under one year of age (43.8%) [3].

First approved in 2023, a maternal vaccine against RSV is now available and indicated for administration during pregnancy to protect infants from RSV-associated dis­ ease in the first months of life [4–7]. Maternal immuni­ zation stimulates the production of pathogen-specific antibodies that are transferred through the placenta and breastmilk, thereby providing early passive immunity to the newborn. Historically, maternal immunization efforts in many countries, including Viet Nam, have centered on tetanus toxoid-containing vaccines, which can be admin­ istered at any point during pregnancy [8]. Viet Nam’s Maternal Neonatal Tetanus Program, introduced in 1993, emphasized maternal vaccination and achieved substan­ tial public health impact, contributing to the elimination of neonatal tetanus in 2005 [9].

Building on this foundation, Viet Nam is expanding maternal immunization efforts. Supported by a strong antenatal care (ANC) system and decades of experi­ ence with maternal vaccines, a limited introduction of the maternal RSV vaccine began in September 2025 through the private-sector, specifically through tertiarylevel providers at Viet Nam Vaccine Joint Stock Company (VNVC) Vaccine Centers and Tam Anh General Hospital Group in Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City [10–12]. Broader rollout to public-sector and lower-level health facilities, as well as to other regions across Viet Nam, has not yet been reported.

Unlike previous maternal vaccines, administration of the RSV vaccine is recommended at specific gestational ages (GAs) in pregnancy. Guidelines for vaccine eligibil­ ity differ across authorities. In Viet Nam, VNVC and Tam Anh facilities currently administer the maternal RSV vac­ cine between 24 and 36 weeks’ gestation [11, 13]. The

World Health Organization (WHO) Strategic Advisory Group of Experts on Immunization (SAGE) recommends vaccination during the third trimester of pregnancy, as defined by the local context (typically at 28 weeks onward, using the Global Alignment of Immunization Safety Assessment [GAIA] definitions of third trimester) [14, 15]. As Viet Nam considers expanding their maternal RSV immunization program, the time-bound adminis­ tration requirements of the vaccine will have operational implications and may also be impacted by the country’s transition to fully self-financing new vaccine introduc­ tions following the conclusion of support from Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance as of 2020 [16].

While ANC in Viet Nam is accessed across multiple levels of care and sectors, little is known about the GA patterns at ANC visits in Viet Nam by level of care within the health system or how the timing of visits aligns with vaccine eligibility windows. Likewise, data are lacking on the daily visit volume of vaccine-eligible women, though both are important for planning effective service deliv­ ery. The objectives of this study were to characterize the distribution of GAs by ANC visits across levels of care and characterize the daily volume of ANC visits made to study facilities by pregnant women at RSV vaccine eligi­ ble GAs.

Methods Study design and sites This retrospective, cross-sectional study was conducted by PATH and Pasteur Institute Nha Trang from Novem­ ber to December 2024 (before the maternal RSV vaccine was introduced in the country), using a standardized study protocol and data collection tools developed by PATH in collaboration with WHO. The study included 15 health facilities across Phu Yen and Khanh Hoa prov­ inces in Viet Nam, selected to capture diversity in level of care, ANC clinic volume, and sociodemographic con­ text. Facilities spanned the primary (commune health facilities, n = 10), secondary (district health facilities, n = 2; specialized maternal health center, n = 1) and ter­ tiary (hospitals, n = 2; one public and one private) levels of care.

Study population Eligible participants were pregnant women attending at least one ANC visit at a study facility during 2023. Records were included if they contained a documented date for the first ANC visit and the GA for at least one visit. We excluded women with multiple pregnancies in the study period, reported negative birth outcomes

Data sources and collection Data were abstracted from ANC registers using approaches tailored to register organization and format. At the primary level, ANC registers were paper-based and organized by individual, with all visits recorded together rather than by visit date. To manage feasibility while maintaining representativeness, we applied a sys­ tematic random sampling approach. Register entries were grouped into consecutive blocks of five women, and one of every two consecutive blocks was selected for inclu­ sion in the study using a random number. Women were included if they attended at least one ANC visit in 2023, encompassing visits occurring from May 2022 through July 2024.

At secondary-level facilities using paper-based, date-organized registers (district health centers at the

secondary level, n = 2), all eligible women attending ANC at the study facility on five randomly selected weekdays per month in 2023 were included. Holidays and week­ ends were excluded to reflect facility closures and the unavailability of maternal vaccine services on those days.

At facilities using electronic ANC registers (one sec­ ondary and two tertiary facilities, n = 3), all ANC visits recorded in 2023 were included without sampling.

Further details on facility characteristics, register types, and data abstraction approaches are provided in Table 1.

Variables and data management Variables abstracted from ANC registers included the date of each ANC visit and the corresponding GA. GA recorded in the register was estimated by health provid­ ers using the date of last menstrual period, fundal height, and estimated date of delivery; ultrasound may have been used in some tertiary facilities. These data were used to characterize the distribution of GA at ANC visits.

Data from paper-based registers were entered into Kobo Toolbox, a digital data capture platform designed to reduce transcription errors and streamline data entry. Unique identifiers were not available in all ANC registers and were not collected. All data were stored on a secure, password-protected server to ensure confidentiality.

Data analysis We use descriptive statistics to describe key variables. GA in weeks are reported as median (interquartile range, IQR). The distribution of GA at ANC visits and the daily number of vaccine-eligible women attending ANC at each facility are visualized by boxplots and bar charts. Analyses evaluated whether pregnant women attended ANC at GAs eligible for RSV vaccination (“vaccine-eli­ gible”) under two eligibility definitions: the current Viet Nam practice (24–36 weeks’ gestation) and the WHO recommendation of vaccination during the third tri­ mester (≥ 28 weeks’ gestation, using GAIA definitions of trimester).

Tables and figures summarize ANC attendance pat­ terns and vaccine eligibility by level of care and eligibil­ ity windows. Since unique identifiers were not available across facilities, ANC visit counts—including first ANC visit (ANC1)—reflect visits recorded within individual facilities and do not capture complete ANC utilization across pregnancy for women receiving care at multiple sites. All analyses were performed using R Statistical

Software, version 4.3 (R Foundation for Statistical Com­ puting, Vienna, Austria).

Results A total of 7,349 women met the inclusion criteria for the primary objective of characterizing GA at ANC vis­ its across levels of care within the health system. Most records (85%) were derived from tertiary-level hospitals using electronic ANC registers. The mean age of preg­ nant women was similar across levels of care, averaging from 26.7 years (SD, 5.8) in primary facilities to 28.5 years (SD, 5.3) in tertiary facilities (Table 2). The timing of the first recorded ANC visit differed by level of care. At pri­ mary facilities, the median GA at the first recorded visit occurred during the first trimester (13 weeks), whereas first recorded visits at secondary and tertiary facilities occurred later in pregnancy with median GAs of 38 and 32 weeks, respectively (Table 2).

Patterns of ANC attendance by trimester differed by level of care (Table  3). Attendance in the first trimes­ ter was highest in primary facilities (52.4%) and lowest in secondary facilities (7.7%). The majority of women attending secondary- and tertiary-level facilities had least one ANC visit during the third trimester (84.8% and 69.2%, respectively). At primary facilities, trimester attendance was highest during the second trimester.

The proportion of women with at least one eligible visit was highest at primary facilities (46.7%), followed by tertiary (35.6%) and secondary facilities (25.6%) (Fig. 1).

Applying the WHO recommendation of vaccina­ tion during the third trimester (≥ 28 weeks’ gestation) increased the proportion of women attending ANC at eli­ gible GAs across all levels of care. Under this definition, 87.7% of women at primary facilities, 84.8% at secondary facilities, and 69.2% at tertiary facilities had at least one eligible ANC visit (Fig. 1).

Attendance prior to RSV eligibility also varied by level of care. Under the current Viet Nam eligibility window, between 15.5% and 40.8% of women attended ANC before reaching vaccine-eligible GAs, with the highest proportion observed at primary facilities. These propor­ tions increased when applying the WHO eligibility defi­ nition, particularly at primary and tertiary level facilities (91.5% primary; 18.6% secondary; 43.7% tertiary) (Fig. 1).

The distribution of GA across ANC visits differed by level of care (Fig.  2). At primary facilities, women attended both their first and second recorded ANC visit at GAs occurring prior to both the current Viet Nam and WHO RSV vaccine eligibility windows, with median GAs 13 and 22 weeks, respectively. At secondary- and

tertiary-level facilities, the first recorded ANC visit gen­ erally occurred during the third trimester.

Primary facilities had substantially higher adherence (62.4%) to the WHO’s Focused Antenatal Care guidelines that were introduced in the early 2000s [17] and recom­ mended a minimum of four targeted visits per pregnancy than secondary (1.1%) and tertiary levels (19.5%). Adher­ ence to the more recent 2016 WHO Recommendations for a Positive Pregnancy Experience  [18], which recom­ mends eight visits per pregnancy, was low in both pri­ mary and tertiary facilities ( 4.1% and 5.5%, respectively); no women recorded more than four ANC visits in sec­ ondary study facilities (Fig. 2).

Women attending primary facilities had a median of four recorded ANC visits; two visits aligning with Viet Nam and WHO-recommended RSV vaccine eligibil­ ity windows (Table  4). At higher levels of care, women had a median of one recorded ANC visit generally fall­ ing within the third trimester (WHO-recommended RSV vaccine eligibility window), but not within the Viet Namdefined RSV vaccine eligibility window (Table 4).

The secondary objective—estimating the daily number of women attending ANC at vaccine-eligible GAs—was assessed in five facilities (Fig.  3). District health cen­ ters (Health Facility [HF] 1 and HF2) received a median of one to two women at vaccine-eligible GAs per day, depending on the vaccine eligibility criteria applied. Discussion This study is, to our knowledge, the first to empirically examine how ANC contact patterns across multiple levels of care align with maternal RSV vaccine eligibil­ ity windows in Viet Nam. Conducted prior to the lim­ ited introduction of the maternal RSV vaccine in Viet Nam, this analysis provides a baseline assessment of routine ANC delivery patterns using facility-based records. By characterizing the timing and frequency of ANC visits at primary, secondary, and tertiary facilities, we identify structural features of ANC service deliv­ ery that are directly relevant for planning maternal RSV

The central finding is that maternal RSV vaccine eligi­ bility criteria and level of care substantially shape the pro­ portion of women who could be reached through existing ANC platforms. Applying the WHO-recommended third trimester definition markedly increased the proportion of women with at least one vaccine-eligible visit across all levels of care (primary, 88%; secondary, 85%; tertiary, 69%) compared with the narrower 24–36-week window currently used in Viet Nam (primary, 47%; secondary, 26%; tertiary, 36%). Although individual women’s com­ plete ANC trajectories may not have been fully captured, particularly if care occurred across multiple facilities or outside study sites, the magnitude and consistency of these differences indicate that eligibility criteria func­ tion as a policy lever. The choice of GA eligibility window directly shapes the potential reach of maternal RSV vac­ cination through routine services.

These findings align with prior modeling and interna­ tional analyses demonstrating that RSV vaccine coverage varies depending on the GA eligibility window applied. Baral et al. estimated approximately 70% coverage in

Viet Nam using the 24- to 36-week window currently used in the country, a projection closer to the atten­ dance observed under the broader ≥ 28-week definition in our data [18]. Studies in Kenya and multi-country analyses similarly show differences in attendance pro­ portions across alternative eligibility windows. Nyiro et al. reported that 63% of women attended ANC between 28 and 32 weeks GA and 59% between 24 and 36 weeks GA [19], while Ford et al. showed greater coverage (79%) using the 24- to 36-week GA window compared with a 28- to 36-week GA window across multiple countries (67%) [20]. Together, these findings reinforce that eligibil­ ity definitions and care-seeking patterns must be consid­ ered jointly to determine achievable coverage.

Understanding how eligibility translates into vacci­ nation opportunities requires examining differences in ANC timing across levels of care. At the primary level, women had an earlier median GA at first recorded ANC visit (13 weeks) and more frequent documented visits (median four) than higher-level facilities. This pattern is consistent with national guidance encouraging early registration at commune health stations and referral of higher-risk pregnancies upward [21]. Primary facilities

therefore serve as recurring points of contact throughout pregnancy. In contrast, secondary and tertiary facilities more often documented first recorded visits at later GAs and fewer visits overall. These differences indicate that vaccination opportunity is structured not only by eligibil­ ity definition but also by where women access care at dif­ ferent stages of pregnancy.

The interaction between eligibility window and care patterns by level of care has operational implications. Under the narrower 24–36 week window, eligibility is more sensitive to the timing of individual visits, par­ ticularly at facilities where women are seen later or less frequently. The broader ≥ 28 week definition increases the likelihood that a routine contact will coincide with vaccine eligibility across levels of care. Daily atten­ dance volumes further shape feasibility. Tertiary hospi­ tals consistently recorded the highest daily volumes of vaccine-eligible women. This finding was anticipated, as secondary facilities are more commonly accessed for episodic or acute services, whereas hospitals represent a subsequent and more consistent site for providing ANC, as reflected in both national data and our findings [22]. Applying the ≥ 28 week definition increased these daily volumes by 1 visits per day in secondary facilities and 5–9 visits per day in tertiary facilities, reflecting both broader eligibility and larger overall patient loads at the tertiary level. Adoption of a broader eligibility window would therefore expand potential reach while simultaneously increasing the number of women eligible for vaccination at high-volume sites, requiring corresponding adjust­ ments in vaccine supply, staffing, and workflow planning. Lower-volume facilities may require different microplan­ ning approaches tailored to predictable but smaller num­ bers of eligible women.

Operational feasibility also differs structurally across levels of care. At the primary level of care we found rou­ tine ANC visits occur more frequently than at higher levels of care, though daily vaccine-eligible volumes could not be quantified for this level. Existing evidence from Viet Nam highlights persistent infrastructure and workforce constraints at primary-level facilities, includ­ ing limited on-site cold-chain capacity, small health care teams, and reliance on coordinated supply delivery from higher-level facilities [23, 24]. These constraints have direct implications for the feasibility of same-day maternal RSV vaccination, particularly in ensuring reli­ able vaccine availability and adequate time for counsel­ ing during routine ANC visits. Hospitals may have more existing resources to support on-site storage, accommo­ date higher staffing needs, and integrated service deliv­ ery, which may facilitate vaccination during eligible visits at scale. Maternal RSV vaccination planning must there­ fore be tailored to the level of care: the number of eligi­ ble women, timing of contacts, and operational capacity

differ across levels of care, and uniform delivery strate­ gies may not be appropriate.

Differences across sectors further extend this argu­ ment. In an ad hoc comparison of the two tertiary care facilities included in this study—one private and one public—women attending the private facility had an ear­ lier median GA at first recorded visit (median 25 weeks) and more documented visits (median two visits) than those attending the public facility, where first recorded visits occurred later and were fewer in number (median 37 weeks at first recorded visit, median one visit total). Although limited to two sites, these observations are consistent with documented differences in care-seeking pathways between public and private sectors in Viet Nam [22] and is relevant for consideration in maternal RSV vaccination planning.

These sectoral differences have direct implications for how vaccine eligibility policy translates into access. Ear­ lier presentation at private tertiary facilities could facili­ tate maternal RSV vaccine delivery under narrower GA eligibility windows, while later presentation at public facilities could limit access without broader eligibility criteria or adaptations to current delivery strategies. In this context, eligibility definitions interact not only with level of care but also with sector-specific care patterns, potentially shaping who is reached during early phases of vaccine introduction. This has important implications for broader rollout strategy and equity. Targeted outreach and education will likely be needed to reach women seeking care in the public sector, alongside coordinated delivery strategies that account for movement between sectors.

These findings highlight the need for coordinated maternal RSV vaccination strategies that account for care-seeking across the full range of facility levels and types. Primary level facilities are often the first point of contact in pregnancy, making them a critical setting for early education and demand generation for maternal RSV vaccination. Although many women initially present within the first trimester, primary care facilities also con­ tinue to see women later in pregnancy when they would be eligible to receive the vaccine. In contrast, higher-level facilities tend to see women later in pregnancy and often only once, generally within the vaccination eligibility period. As a result, these facilities must prioritize readi­ ness for same-day vaccination to avoid missed opportu­ nities. Across all levels of care, linked health records are essential to ensure continuity: integrated systems help prevent inadvertent revaccination while also ensuring that women are not missed for vaccination as they move between facilities and levels of the health system.

Given that Viet Nam has not yet rolled out the mater­ nal RSV vaccine in the public sector, these data provide timely evidence to inform policy decisions. Revisiting

the eligibility window for maternal RSV vaccination from the current 24- to 36-weeks’ GA to the third trimester (≥ 28-week GA) could substantially increase coverage and protect more infants. Optimizing maternal RSV cover­ age will require adapting education and service delivery strategies to the realities of care-seeking behavior and ensuring robust health information systems that support continuity of care across all facility types and sectors.

One strength of this study is the use of real-world ANC register data from diverse facility levels, capturing patient and provider practices rather than relying on modeled estimates. Collecting data after the peak of COVID-19 service disruptions and excluding clinic closure days allowed for realistic estimates of ANC service volumes. Data completeness was also high; GA was available for every ANC visit recorded in the study period in all study facilities.

Our study has several limitations. The absence of unique patient identifiers in ANC registers made it impossible to track women across health facilities. As in most countries, the tiered maternal health system in Viet Nam accommodates women seeking care at mul­ tiple facilities during a single pregnancy. Consequently, facility-based records may reflect episodic service con­ tacts rather than individual care pathways, resulting in estimates that reflect patterns of service utilization at the facility level rather than individual-level timing of care initiation and follow up. Also, due to changing elec­ tronic register ownership and record accessibility, data from tertiary facilities were restricted to a single calen­ dar year, 2023, while lower-levels of care included data from 2022 to 2024, thus limiting the direct comparabil­ ity of ANC timing patterns between levels of care. While we addressed within-facility selection bias through ran­ dom sampling at facilities with paper-based records and included all women at facilities with electronic registers, the overall data overrepresents women attending tertiary care, who may differ systematically from women at lower levels of care. Finally, by including only women with documented ANC visits, our findings may overestimate potential RSV vaccine coverage at the population level.

Conclusions This research underscores the importance of aligning maternal RSV immunization strategies with ANC atten­ dance patterns across levels of the health system in Viet Nam. Timing and frequency of ANC visits play a cen­ tral role in shaping vaccine opportunity, and observed differences by level of care highlight the need for tar­ geted delivery strategies. Focusing vaccination counsel­ ing and education efforts on primary facilities will be particularly important in Viet Nam because these set­ tings consistently demonstrate earlier and more regu­ lar engagement of women attending ANC. Aligning

national GA eligibility guidance with observed ANC attendance, particularly adoption of the WHO-recom­ mended ≥ 28-week eligibility window, could substantially expand opportunities for RSV vaccination within existing service delivery platforms. Achieving high and equitable coverage will require translating these opportunities into practice through strengthening early ANC engagement and counseling, tailored scheduling and logistics based on facility-level attendance patterns, and expansion of access beyond the private sector to public facilities. Investment in integrated digital health information sys­ tems that support the continuity of ANC records across facilities would further strengthen program planning and help ensure women have opportunities to receive mater­ nal RSV vaccination regardless of where care is sought. Collectively, these actions can support effective, efficient, and equitable national rollout of maternal RSV vaccine in Viet Nam.
